subject: Fuaran-Core
$comment: This repository's claims ladder, declared as data. It is `proofs/README.md`'s own ladder — what is PROVED, what is only TESTED, what is ASSUMED — in a schema a tool can read, so the question does not have to be answered by reading prose and hoping two documents use the same words. A `not claimed` item is the ABSENCE of a row, never a row: the README enumerates those, and enumerating them here would turn a disclaimer into a claim. Levels are the closed set proved | tested | assumed | policy. Authored by hand, never generated — editing the ladder means editing this file and the README together. Since Phase 144 it is CHECKED rather than trusted: the proof leg's host step runs the `Proofs.Ladder` family (tests/Fuaran.Core.Tests/ProofsLadderTests.fs), which holds every row to the tree — a proved row's theorem is a top-level declaration of the model it names, that model is one `proofs/check.ps1` actually checks, a tested row's named cases exist in the `Proofs.Oracle` family, every checked module has a proved row, and the phase citations and levels are the closed forms. Row-to-tree agreement only: whether a row says the same thing as the README's prose stays a human act.

claims.claim: On the model, for every N and every permutation of a lane set, the fold halts with the same canonical conflict report or folds to the same state. Proved with no assume and no admit under --report_assumes error; the fold half under `independence_diamond` for a lane set whose lanes all apply from the base, the halt half under no hypothesis at all.
Every decode combinator reaches exactly one outcome on every input, and which one is characterised structurally — so the failure classification is exhaustive rather than merely non-empty.

The recursive node decoder is total on an arbitrary JSON value and succeeds on exactly the well-formed documents. Termination is content here rather than a formality: the decoder descends into a child array obtained by name, so nothing structural is visible at the call site.
Decoding an encoded node returns that node, for every node of the reference vocabulary, at every depth.

On every document the read policy does not name, the tolerant and strict readers accept the same values and refuse the same documents — a promise about the VERDICT, not about the message; on a document with no null at all the two are literally the same function.

Production's delta recovery from a content-addressed DAG, its pairwise conflict sweep, the composition and the replay together agree with the extracted model over three lane pools, per lane set and per sampled arrival order — outcome and composed merge script, not merely a hash. Agreement is over the sets drawn and the orders enumerated, never over all inputs.

Sampled — never proved — including directly against the extracted model's own independence predicate on the reference witness, with a sample-adequacy guard and its own go-red. Hashing is abstracted behind an opaque minting function; what it buys is stated separately as `node-ids-distinct`. The ancestor closure, the difference against the base's closure, the lookup and the fold built on them are no longer assumed: see `dag-delta-recovery` and `fold-from-the-dag`.

The near-miss tokens that make this an assumption rather than a theorem are grammar, and stay with the parser; the differential is the evidence for it, not a proof of it.

claims.claim: Which prover is pinned, how many cold-cache runs a check is, and that a model edited without re-extracting fails the leg — the reproducibility posture the proved rows above are only as good as. Policy, not algebra: no theorem addresses it. Since Phase 148 the posture also says what the leg COSTS: each module's cold-run budget is declared in proofs/modules.json, measured on every run and printed beside the measurement, with an overshoot named as a warning — prover time varies by machine and by load, so it is a smoke detector rather than a gate — and `check.ps1 -Strict` for a session that wants one red. The numbers live there rather than in a row here, because a wall-clock budget is a claim at none of this ladder's four levels and is per module where a row is per claim.

For the base-plus-N-chains shape — one shared base node and one linear chain per writer, which is what the fold's own generator builds and what a local-first deployment has — the delta of a lane off the base is that lane's nodes, and its ops, in append order. The whole layer computed rather than assumed: the head's ancestor closure, the base's, the topological order, the difference and the lookup. Under the id-distinctness premise; the CHOICE of topological order was named separately as an assumption here and is PROVED since Phase 142, at `topological-order-choice`.

The fold over the DAG is the fold over the lane lists, and the confluence law therefore holds stated from the content-addressed DAG rather than from deltas someone had already recovered: the same heads over the same base fold to the same state, or halt with the same canonical report, however the heads arrive.

Production's own ancestor closure, topological order and delta recovery, on the DAG the fold's generator actually builds, agree per lane with the extracted model's recovery over the SAME nodes across three lane pools — the ids the model walks are the content hashes production minted, so a disagreement can only be about the recovery and never about the hash. A DAG whose lanes hang off the wrong parent is required to make the comparison fail, and two vacuity guards refuse a run that recovered no ops or walked no chain longer than one node.

claims.claim: The hash-collision assumption, and since Phase 134 the only thing the delta recovery assumes about content addressing. Node ids are distinct, so the node a chain named is the node the DAG returns for it; two nodes sharing a content id is the only way that fails.

evidence.assumption: Dag.nodeHash is injective on (sorted parents, actor, encoded op)

claims.claim: That the order production picks and the order the model computes are the same order, on the base-plus-N-chains shape. Two lemmas: a distinct enumeration of a spine's closure in which every node follows its single parent is that spine in append order (`spine_order_forced`, a list argument naming no DAG and no hash), and the frontier drain over that closure produces such an enumeration (`kahn_drain_is_such_an_enumeration`). The recovery is therefore restated with the order universally quantified rather than fixed to the parent-walk reversal (`between_chain_any_order`), and the fold above it with it (`reconcile_many_dag_ordered_eq`, `fold_once_dag_ordered_eq`). The smallest-id tie-break is NOT modelled and does not need to be: the selector is a parameter constrained only to return a member of the frontier it is handed, and on a spine that frontier is one element wide at every step (`kahn_frontier_singleton`), so every selector agrees and nothing here says how ids compare. The order over a MERGE DAG, where the frontier genuinely widens, remains unclaimed at any level.

For the skeleton-op tree algebra, two operations whose footprints are declared disjoint and which both apply at an id-unique tree each apply after the other and reach the same tree — the fold theorem's domain hypothesis, proved rather than sampled, for twelve of the fifteen unordered operation pairs (the three left open are one shape, at `tree-algebra-batch-nesting`). Nine of the twelve are closed by the conservative footprint alone and never look at a tree: a remove or a move writes an unknown parent, independence refuses that against any structural write, and every skeleton operation except a do-nothing batch writes structure — so such a pair is independent only where the other operation does nothing at all.

The unknown-parent over-approximation in `Ops.independent` is NECESSARY over the `Footprint` record as it stands, not merely conservative: no predicate over the four address sets can widen the promise. Proved at one well-formed tree by three facts — a relocation that MOVES a node and a structural write under a parent inside the moved subtree do commute, with every clause but the pinned relocation pair already satisfied (`relocation_disjoint_diamond`); the same shape with a REMOVE in it does not, because the structural write's parent is destroyed with the subtree (`relocation_diamond_fails_for_a_remove`); and the two operations carry byte-identical footprints (`relocation_footprints_coincide`). One verdict therefore covers both, so freeing the safe pair frees the fatal one. A single witness refutes the universal claim. This is also the second pinned over-approximation — a remove's content-write records the target id and not its tree-unknown subtree — shown to be load-bearing for the first, which STABILITY.md had asserted in prose since Phase 78. NOT claimed: anything about what a WIDER record would admit, or the general move-versus-structural-write theorem, which is true and deliberately unproved because no clause could consume it.

The pairs the pinned clause refuses, enumerated: exactly {a relocating operation} x {an operation that is not inert}, both ways round — `still_refused`, the contrapositive of `relocating_forces_inert`. Part of that set is GENUINELY dependent and could not be freed by any footprint record whatever: two `MoveNode`s whose destinations sit inside each other's subtrees each apply alone and reject each other with `WouldNestUnderSelf`, because the obstruction is the cycle check rather than the addresses (`relocation_move_pair_also_fails`). So the refused set is not one homogeneous class waiting on a better footprint. No claim is made here about the remove-versus-remove, remove-versus-move or remove-versus-reorder members, which Phase 143 did not examine.

The precision-ceiling witness run on the EXTRACTED model and on production `Ops.footprint` / `Ops.independent` / `Ops.apply` side by side, over the reference domain: the same two operations are footprint-indistinguishable in both, both refuse the pair, the move commutes in both and the remove-shaped batch diverges in both. A decision not to change something survives only as a check that goes red when someone does, and this is that check. Agreement is over this witness, never over all inputs.

tests: the pinned unknown-parent clause is necessary — both classes, on the model and on production

claims.claim: Fold confluence for the skeleton-op tree algebra with NO domain hypothesis remaining, over the non-batch operation alphabet: the same lanes reach the same tree however they arrive, a lane set that cannot fold halts with the same canonical report however it arrives, and none folds under one order and halts under another. The halt half is proved separately under no hypothesis at all — not the diamond, not id uniqueness, nothing about the apply engine.

HISTORICAL SINCE PHASE 138, and kept rather than deleted. Phase 133 refuted the unconditional statement 'every accepted skeleton operation preserves id uniqueness' against the validator of the day: it tested the inserted node's OWN id against the tree and not its descendants, so a concrete accepted insert left the tree carrying an id twice. Phase 137 fixed the validator and Phase 138 lifted the model to it, so this is no longer a claim about the LIVE algebra — the counterexample and the clause it is about are named `insert_breaks_wf_pre137` and `apply_pre137`, and the refutation stands exactly as it did. What it refuted is now TRUE and proved, at `apply-preserves-wf`; that the fix closes THIS counterexample is proved at `insert-subtree-check-closes-it`. Proved beside it throughout, and unchanged: the conditional form `ins_wf` and its converse `ins_wf_conv`, which were the specification the fix had to meet.

The extracted tree model agrees with the shipped apply engine and footprint derivation over the generated operation pool and every state a prefix of it reaches — the footprint as four address sets, the verdict, an accepted result through the content hash computed by production's own function on both sides, and a rejection by class. Every rejection class the plain apply can raise is asserted reached BY NAME rather than counted, and a bridge that erases every kind tag is required to make the result comparison fail, so a green report is known to be one that can lose.

tests: the tree oracle agrees with Ops.apply and Ops.footprint over the generated pool
a tree oracle handed a blind bridge DISAGREES with Ops.apply
the extracted tree model keeps the diamond its own theorem proves
a blind footprint BREAKS the extracted model's diamond — the measurement can fail

claims.claim: The tree the algebra runs over carries each id at most once. This is a hypothesis rather than an oversight: the lookup that resolves an id returns the FIRST match in document order, so on a tree carrying one id twice what it returns is a fact about the order as well as the contents — and a reorder moves the order, which makes the diamond FALSE there rather than merely unproved. Nothing in the estate produces such a tree and the structural diff refuses one outright, but no shipped type carries the invariant. NARROWED BY PHASE 138 to what it now is — a hypothesis about the INPUT alone. Until Phase 137 the algebra could also break the invariant on a tree that had it (`insert-breaks-id-uniqueness`); since Phase 138 that half is a theorem, `apply-preserves-wf`, so a tree that starts id-unique stays id-unique under every accepted operation. What remains unenforced is the entry point, and only the entry point.

evidence.assumption: the tree the fold runs over carries each id at most once

claims.claim: The proved diamond covers twelve of the fifteen operation pairs; the three left open are one shape — either side a batch that neither does nothing nor relocates. A batch is a list of operations written as one operation and the fold already threads a list, so excluding it removes no behaviour: it declines to nest one lane inside another. Lifting the leaf diamond along a batch script is the argument the fold theorem already performs at lane granularity, and it needs the id-uniqueness invariant at each intermediate state of the script. PHASE 138 SUPPLIES THAT INVARIANT and does not perform the lift: `apply-preserves-wf` is exactly the missing hypothesis, so this boundary is now unblocked rather than blocked, and the three pairs stay open because nobody has done the induction. That is a different statement from the one this row carried, and the distinction is the point — a boundary waiting on a theorem and a boundary waiting on labour are not the same debt.

evidence.assumption: an operation pair in which either side is a non-trivial nested batch

claims.claim: A content-addressed DAG grown from nothing by append and merge alone, each naming parents the DAG already held, has no integrity break; and a linear hash chain grown from genesis by append alone verifies. The id half is free by construction, but the parent half is not: append does not check that the parent it is handed names a node the DAG holds, so every-parent-present is a precondition on how a DAG was grown rather than a property of the constructor, and the theorem carries it as one. Its PREMISE is the whole of nothing: `intact_verifies` takes no injectivity hypothesis of any kind — not the hash's, not the codec's, not the splices' — because append mints the id from the content it is storing, so the id cannot be wrong however weak the hash is. Phase 145 left it untouched for that reason; there was nothing there to decompose.

Changing one DAG node's op, actor or parent multiset while leaving its address as it was, in a DAG whose node under that id was intact, is reported as a break; and the same for one linear record's sequence, actor or op with its two hash fields left alone. Both are corollaries of a characterisation of the walker itself: the walk finds nothing exactly when every key is its content hash and every named parent is present, and exactly when every record's sequence, prev-link and recomputed hash agree. Since Phase 145 the DAG arm's premise is `node_injective_on`, which is the Phase 136 composite RESTRICTED to pre-images whose parents are ids and whose actor string is one the actor code emits — what the splice lemmas need, and what production supplies, since a stored parent is a key of the map or the walk's second clause reports it and a stored actor is an Actor the walker re-encodes. A caller builds that premise from the two that remain assumptions, through `node_injective_derived`; the linear arm's `rec_injective` is still the bundled Phase 136 form.

Three break classes are proved under NO hypothesis at all, which is the sharpest thing the mechanisation says: a linear record renumbered, a linear record re-pointed at a different predecessor, and a DAG node another node names being absent. Those three checks compare stored data against the walk's own running values or against the key set, and never consult the hash — so they are detectable independently of the hash's strength. Only the recomputed-hash check spends the cryptographic premise.

merge(A,B) and merge(B,A) converge to one content id, because the parents are sorted before hashing. Needs only that the comparison is a total order and nothing about the hash. Its converse is proved too and is a boundary rather than a result: re-ordering a node's parents is NOT a detectable tamper, and is not meant to be.

The extracted model agrees with Dag.firstBreak and OpStream.firstChainBreak over generated DAGs and chains and every single-node tamper of each, comparing the verdict, the location, WHICH check failed and the expected and got values at once — and mints production's own content ids node by node, which is checkable only through append because nodeHash is private. Two go-red cases require a model handed a different hash to disagree, and a third runs one tamper under two hashes: found under the real one, INVISIBLE under a deliberately non-injective one, to production and to the model alike. Every run asserts that detection actually happened, because two walkers that both say intact agree perfectly and certify nothing.

claims.claim: The cryptographic premise, and since Phase 145 the only claim about the DAG's content id that is assumed rather than proved or certified: two (key, value) pairs that mint one digest are the same pair. It is an explicit lemma-valued PARAMETER (`hash_injective`) of the theorems that need it rather than an assume, so which results depend on it is visible in their signatures. Phase 136 stated it in a bundled form that also carried the two splices and the op codec; those are now `preimage-splices-unambiguous` and `op-codec-injective-certified` below, and this row is what is left. It is still stated MODULO THE PARENT SORT, which is the strongest true form. The LINEAR side's `rec_injective` is NOT decomposed and remains bundled — its pre-image is a four-way JSON envelope rather than nodeHash's two splices, and decomposing it is separate work, named here rather than implied.

evidence.assumption: the HashFn is injective on the (key, value) pairs it is handed; and, on the linear side only, the chain payload hash is injective on the pre-images that occur

claims.claim: The two SPLICES in `Dag.nodeHash`'s pre-image are unambiguous, and the composite premise the tamper theorems take is therefore DERIVED from the hash's own injectivity and the op codec's rather than assumed alongside them. `parent_splice_unambiguous`: `String.concat ","` is injective on lists of parent ids, given that an id carries no comma and is not empty — both conditions load-bearing, since `["a,b"]` and `["a";"b"]` join alike without the first and `[]` and `[""]` do without the second. `actor_op_splice_unambiguous`: `actor ^ "|" ^ encodedOp` recovers both halves, given that neither actor encoding is a proper prefix of the other. That second condition is NOT the separator-freedom Phase 136's README named, which is false of production: `Actor.encode` does not escape the pipe, so a Human whose id is `a|b` encodes with one in it. What is true is stronger — a JSON object whose string literals are self-delimiting is a prefix-free code — and it is what the lemma takes. The reading of a string as its symbols is a stated hypothesis (`symbols_faithful`) in the same style as `total_order`, not a parameter: concatenation is symbol-list append and two strings with the same symbols are the same string.

The fourth thing Phase 136's premise bundled: the op codec is injective. It is the DOMAIN'S — `StreamWitness.Encode` belongs to whoever brings the op type — so the model takes it as a parameter (`op_codec_injective`) and the kit carries the law a witness certifies it with (`Conformance.codecInjectivityLaws`), the same division the fold theorem's `independence_diamond` runs on. Three arms: no collision drawn, the codec has a left inverse (`Decode ∘ Encode = Ok`, which makes it injective rather than merely un-collided, and which one drawn op exercises where a collision search needs the pair), and the draw compared more than one encoding. Certified here for the work-plan witness the DAG and chain differentials themselves run on. The two alphabet conditions the splice lemmas ask of production are measured beside it, over an adversarial actor population rather than a typical one, with both directions probed: a bare-id encoder is prefix-comparable and DOES collide on the same population, and a codec that erases its op makes a tamper invisible to production's own walker with the hash untouched.

tests: an actor encoding CAN carry the splice separator — Phase 136's stated reason is REFUTED
Actor.encode is a PREFIX-FREE code — the premise the splice lemma actually takes
the actor/op splice recovers both halves over the adversarial population
a content id carries no comma and is not empty, and a parent id that would names no node
the op codec this differential runs on certifies injective through the kit's own law

claims.claim: That the order the model walks is the order production walks. Production enumerates Map.toList, which is ascending key order; the model walks the list it is given, and the differential hands it exactly that list. The VERDICT is order-independent by construction — a break exists or it does not — so only which break is reported first depends on this, and nothing here is said about F#'s Map enumeration.

evidence.assumption: the entry list the model is handed is Map.toList's own order

claims.claim: The recursive-descent JSON parser reaches exactly one outcome on every input — an accepted value or a CLASSIFIED refusal, never both and never neither. That it is Tot at all is the content rather than a formality: F* admits the mutual group only after showing it terminates on every input, and a recursive-descent parser over a mutable index has no syntactic reason to. Every consuming sub-parser carries the remaining input's strict decrease in its RETURN TYPE, and that refinement is the whole termination argument.

On the canonical nesting family the depth bound is EXACT at every depth and for every suffix: the parse succeeds iff the cap is at least the nesting, and refuses by name when it is not. Stated this way because the obvious form is false — the parser is left to right and the first failure wins, so a document that is both too deep and malformed earlier fails with the earlier kind. The other two halves are depth_error_only_at_a_container (the kind is confined to a container position, carried in every signature's return type so it is re-checked at every call site) and depth_bound_scalars_unaffected (a scalar parses at a cap of zero, where every container is refused).

Every integer token the parser ACCEPTS denotes an int53-safe value, whichever branch produced it — JInt by the Int32 range, JFloat by the guard. Note where the guard is NOT: the Int32 branch runs no int53 test and needs none, because the Int32 range is a strict subset (int32_within_int53 proves it).

The int53 guard as production spells it — a lexical comparison against the range's own digits — never admits an integer whose VALUE is outside the range. This is the half that matters: over-refusing costs a user an error message, under-refusing costs a corrupted identifier.

The int53 guard is NOT exact, and cannot be as written: Wire.fs justifies its lexical comparison with 'JSON forbids leading zeros', which this parser's digit loop does not enforce, so 0009007199254740992 — exactly 2^53, the largest int53-safe integer there is — is refused as MalformedNumber because its STRING is 19 characters. Proved as a witness rather than described, so that anyone who 'fixes' the guard to match its own comment reddens a lemma and is told the parser's behaviour changed. The error only ever runs this way; soundness above is the other half.

Every one of the twelve JsonErrorKind cases is REACHABLE, by a named witness input — a classification whose cases are unreachable is closed but not exhaustive, and the difference is what makes the differential's coverage mean anything. The confinement half is carried in the parsers' return types rather than asserted once, so it is re-checked at every call site: parse_string cannot report a number failure, the descent cannot report TrailingCharacters (which the entry point constructs from the leftover-input test rather than raising), and MaxDepthExceeded cannot arise anywhere but at a container.

The extracted model agrees with Json.parseDetailedWithPolicy over a 55-input near-miss table under both read policies, every wire-corpus nodes/ and ops/ fixture as raw text, both nesting families at every depth 0-8 under every cap 0-8, arrays and objects up to 64 members, and 4,000 seed-replayable generated inputs — comparing the outcome class, the decoded value, and on a failure the KIND, the POSITION and the MESSAGE at once. Two go-red cases: a model holding a cap production has already spent must accept what production refuses by name, and a blind bridge hiding the two container characters must break every structured document while leaving a scalar in agreement. The member-null fork is asserted to have FIRED, because two parsers that never met a member null agree about a policy neither exercised.

… and under the tolerant read policy, where the member-null fork lives
the parser oracle agrees with production over every corpus nodes/ fixture
… and over every corpus ops/ fixture
the parser oracle agrees with production over generated deep and wide inputs

a model handed a BLIND bridge DISAGREES with production

claims.claim: System.Double.TryParse's three-valued verdict on a number token — parses finitely, parses to a non-finite, does not parse — is a PARAMETER of the model, instantiated by the differential host with the call production makes. What the model decides is which verdict leads where, which is the parser's own logic; nothing here is said about float precision, about which tokens .NET accepts, or about the shortest-round-trip layout. System.Int32.TryParse is likewise modelled lexically, as a comparison against the range's own digits after stripping leading zeros, which is argued rather than mechanised and measured by the differential's boundary cases from both sides.

evidence.assumption: the float readback and the Int32 range test are the host's, not the model's

claims.claim: That the model's character list IS the production string. A character is a constructor of the model's alphabet — one per character the parser distinguishes, plus a catch-all carrying the character verbatim, so two different characters are never identified — and the host's one-line-per-character bridge is what makes the correspondence. The bridge is not itself proved. The value of a \uXXXX escape is on the same footing: the model carries the four hex digits symbolically because the extraction carries no integers, and the host resolves the code point, so the decoded character is compared but the transliteration is sampled rather than proved.

evidence.assumption: the host's toCh bridge maps each production character to the model's alphabet faithfully

claims.claim: The insert graft's uniqueness scan decides EXACTLY the hypothesis the preservation argument needs: it finds nothing precisely when the graft's ids repeat neither the tree's nor each other's. Both directions, and both matter. Left to right is soundness — an accepted graft cannot break the invariant. Right to left is sharpness — a refused graft genuinely would have broken it, so the check refuses nothing safe. Beside it, `wf_iff_no_dups`: the structural well-formedness predicate the preservation arguments are written over and the flat no-duplicates list the scan computes are the same predicate, which was a sentence in a comment until Phase 137's check made it load-bearing.

The concrete accepted insert Phase 133 exhibited as a counterexample is REFUSED by the lifted model, naming the descendant id as the offender. The fix machine-checked at the exact point where the algebra was broken, and a go-red by construction: narrow the validator back and this stops verifying. Its historical twin, `insert_breaks_wf_pre137`, proves the same insert is still admitted by the clause as it stood.

The apply engine reaches exactly one outcome on every operation and every tree — which in the model is the type of the function, discharged by construction — and WHICH rejection each clause can raise is characterised, not listed. The characterisation is the content: `NotAContainer` and `Rejected` are proved unreachable from `apply` (`apply_never_container_or_domain`), where the README asserted it in prose; a `Batch` inherits exactly the union of its members'.

A refused step leaves the caller holding the input tree. For one operation that is a type-level fact of persistent values that no test and no conformance law names; for a script it is the all-or-nothing discipline, and there it has content — the statement is quantified over an ARBITRARY failure position in an arbitrary batch, so however many intermediate trees the prefix built, none of them escapes.

Every accepted operation preserves id uniqueness — unconditionally, for all five skeleton operations including a nested batch. This is the statement Phase 133 REFUTED and could only prove in conditional form, and it is true now because Phase 137 changed the code rather than because the model changed its mind: `validator-decides-the-invariant` is the link between the two. Its remove and move clauses needed machinery Phase 133 never had, principally that a remove takes the whole removed subtree's ids away with it, which is what makes the move's re-insert provably fresh.

The dry run and the mutating call accept exactly the same operations, and what the mutating call then produces is well-formed. The sampled `canApply` = `apply` law becomes a corollary. The part worth naming is what the proof needed: two defensive `UnknownNode` fallbacks the shipped engine carries after its `parentOf` lookup are UNREACHABLE, because a non-root id the tree holds always has a parent — so the two surfaces cannot diverge by one of them taking a branch the other does not.

The inverse of an accepted operation is itself accepted at the result and restores the input exactly, for the four non-batch operations. Both halves in one statement: nothing about the derived inverse can be refused at the tree the forward step produced, and applying it gives back the tree the forward step was applied to. The defining law `apply (invert op pre) (apply op pre) = pre`, which the engine's own doc comment states and the conformance pack samples, is a theorem here. The batch alphabet is excluded and the exclusion is stated: a batch's inverse is its members' inverses in reverse order, each derived against the state that member saw, so the lift is the one the fold theorem already performs at lane granularity.

The extracted preservation model agrees with the shipped `Ops.apply`, `Ops.canApply` and `Ops.invert` over the generated pool AND over grafts minted per state from the state's own ids: a subtree whose descendant id the tree already holds, a subtree that repeats an id within itself, and one that does both. Compared at once: the verdict, an accepted result through production's own `Tree.encodeHash`, a rejection by class, the dry run against the mutating call on each side separately, the derived inverse as an operation, and the round trip run on production. The go-red hands the differential the model of the PRE-137 validator and requires it to lose — which is the same comparison that was silently green throughout Phase 137, because the generator's contract is a fresh id and it cannot mint a colliding graft. Agreement is over the pool drawn, never over all inputs.

claims.claim: The witness laws themselves. The model reads a node as an id, a kind tag and an ordered child list, and treats `ReplaceChildren` as an abstract function satisfying `Conformance.witnessLaws` — exactly as the fold theorem takes the independence diamond abstractly. A domain's own `ReplaceChildren` is that domain's promise, sampled by the conformance pack and proved by nothing; where it does not hold, every theorem above is about a different function from the one that runs. Note the pack's own boundary here: `witnessLaws` exempts a leaf from the round trip, so a witness whose `ReplaceChildren` is partial on leaves is lawful.

That the witness surface is the whole of the tree. `Tree.ids` walks `NodeWitness.Children`, so a node a domain holds in a keyed, non-structural position is invisible to the uniqueness scan, to every theorem above, and to the differential. Uniqueness over those positions is the domain's own obligation. Stated as an assumption rather than a limitation because it is what the theorems quantify over: they are true of the witness view, and the witness view is what `Ops` can see.

evidence.assumption: the domain exposes every node it wants the algebra to see through NodeWitness.Children

claims.claim: The container-aware engine is the plain one plus a guard, and the model of it is faithful clause for clause. At `canHold = fun _ -> true` the two are the SAME FUNCTION — which is what `Ops.apply = applyWith (fun _ -> true)` asserts in the code and nothing checked — and proving it discharges the two lookups the model writes as total matches where the engine writes a fall-through: a parent whose id the tree holds is always found, so neither engine can take a branch the other does not.

`NotAContainer` is exactly the container violation's refusal: `apply` never raises it (Phase 138's characterisation), the container-aware engine differs from `apply` ONLY by raising it, and where it raises it the named node is one the tree holds, the reported kind tag is that node's own, and the predicate refuses it. The middle clause is the one with content — it says the capability can never accept what `apply` refuses, never produce a different tree, and never refuse under another class of its own. Note what it deliberately does NOT say, because the differential's first run is what taught it: the capability can PRE-EMPT another refusal rather than only adding one. A self-move into a leaf is `NotAContainer` here and `WouldNestUnderSelf` under `apply`, because the capability test precedes the descendant test in the shipped `MoveNode` arm — so the theorem reads `identical, or NotAContainer`, and a reading of the form `the same class unless the capability adds one` is false.

`applyContained` preserves the invariant the capability exists to keep — every node with children satisfies `canHold` — for all five operations including a nested batch, with `MoveNode` covered as well as `InsertChild`. The move clause is the one with content: the moved subtree inherits the invariant from the tree it came out of, the removal preserves both the invariant and the destination's capability, and the graft is then an insert under an admitted parent. Two hypotheses are carried and both are REFUTED without them (`contained-premises`), so the theorem is about the function that ships rather than about a cleaner one.

The preservation theorem's two hypotheses are necessary, each by a machine-checked counterexample the module can evaluate — the `insert_breaks_wf_pre137` shape. `contained_needs_child_blind`: `canHold` has type `'Node -> bool`, so it may read the CHILD LIST, and a predicate that does can admit a node at the moment it is checked and refuse it the instant it gains a child — every other hypothesis holds and the invariant breaks anyway. `contained_needs_op_hypothesis`: the engine applies `canHold` to the PARENT and to nothing inside the graft, so inserting a subtree whose own interior node is a non-container carries the violation in with it. Neither is a modelling convenience: each is a property of a real predicate that the engine's type does not demand, and naming them is what makes the theorem about `applyContained` rather than about a function nobody calls.

The container-aware dry run returns exactly what the container-aware mutating call returns, envelope included — `canApplyContained` is `canApplyWith canHold`, sharing the three validators with `applyWith` and simulating the two order-dependent clauses. Phase 138's corollary carries over unchanged and is what the remove clause needs: the `parentOf` fallback the engine carries is unreachable, so the two surfaces cannot diverge by one taking a branch the other does not.

A FINDING about the shipped surface when Phase 140 ran, proved rather than asserted: there was no container-aware SEQUENCE surface. `Ops.canApplyAll` and `Ops.applyAll` both threaded the plain `apply`, so a script `canApplyAll` certified could be refused by `applyContained` at its first step — the counterexample is one move of a leaf under a leaf. A caller that pre-flights with `canApplyAll` and executes with `applyContained`, which is the combination the two doc comments invite, had a check that could not see the refusal its executor would make. Recorded rather than fixed there, because closing it is an API change with a version; the lemma plus its production-side case are what made the gap visible to whoever took it. CLOSED by Phase 160 (`container-sequence-gap-closed`), which added `applyAllWith` / `canApplyAllWith` beside the plain pair. This row is KEPT and its lemma is still true, because its meaning changed rather than expiring: the plain pair is the `fun _ -> true` instance and is therefore blind to containment by construction, so what this now pins is that Phase 160 moved no existing caller.

The extracted container model agrees with the shipped `Ops.applyContained` and `Ops.canApplyContained` over a GENERATED `canHold` — a random subset of the pool's kind vocabulary per trial, including the empty predicate (nothing can hold children) and the total one (where the engine is `apply` again), all eight drawn. A differential run against one hand-picked predicate would certify that instance and nothing about the quantifier the theorems carry. Five comparisons per probe: the verdict and the accepted result through production's own `Tree.encodeHash`, the rejection by class, the dry run against the mutating call on each side, `applyContained` against `apply` on production, and the invariant asserted on production wherever its hypotheses are met. Adequacy is counted per capability SITE — insert refusals, move refusals, batch inheritance and pre-emptions separately — because a run that reached only the insert site could not have caught the go-red, which is a move. The go-red is the model's own instrument: an engine checking the capability on insert and not on move, proved in F* to admit a move the real one refuses, required to lose here. Agreement is over the pool drawn, never over all inputs.

claims.claim: The container invariant survives a SCRIPT under `Ops.applyAllWith`, and survives it on BOTH arms — the accepted tree and the partial tree a refusal hands back. The second arm is what a per-operation theorem structurally cannot state: a refused `applyContained` returns no tree at all, while a refused script keeps the accepted prefix and hands it to the caller, so a preservation statement covering only the accepted case would be silent about precisely the state a non-atomic surface exists to produce. Same two hypotheses as `contained-preserves` (`child_blind` and `contained_op`, both refuted without them by `contained-premises`), over any predicate, any script and any well-formed tree carrying the invariant.

The container-aware sequence dry run returns exactly what the container-aware sequence apply returns — same verdict, same refusal INDEX, same envelope. The index is the half that makes the statement worth having for a script: a pre-flight that agreed on accept-vs-refuse while disagreeing about WHICH step failed would be useless to a caller deciding what to do next. Note what this needs and `canapply-contained-agrees` does: nothing. That one requires `wf t` because the per-operation dry run reaches the three validators directly and must be shown not to take a branch the mutating call does not; the sequence pair cannot diverge that way by construction, since both fold the SAME per-operation call — which is also the honest reading of why the shipped `canApplyAll` threads `apply` rather than `canApply`.

`Ops.applyAll` and `Ops.canApplyAll` ARE the `fun _ -> true` instances of the new pair, so no existing caller's behaviour moved when the capability arrived — the claim an additive API change has to earn, proved rather than asserted. Discharged against `TreeOps.apply_all` and section 8's `can_apply_all`, the two folds as they stood BEFORE Phase 160, so what is proved is agreement with the shipped behaviour rather than with a restatement of itself. The corollary is worth reading as a property rather than as an omission: the plain pair is blind to containment now and always will be, that being what the total instance means, so a caller that pre-flights with `canApplyAll` and executes with `applyContained` still has the Phase 140 gap and now has a surface that closes it.

`container-sequence-gap`'s counterexample, answered. The same script at the same tree: the plain sequence dry run certifies it, and the container-aware one refuses it at index 0 with `NotAContainer("leaf", "para")` — the envelope `applyAllWith` raises — while the mutating call hands the tree back untouched, because the refusal is at the first step and the accepted prefix is empty. The two lemmas are read TOGETHER and the older one is kept rather than retired, because its meaning changed: it was a finding about a missing surface, and it is now the pin that the plain pair's behaviour did not move. What Phase 160 closed is the absence of ANY container-aware sequence surface, not the plain pair's blindness — the plain pair is blind by construction, and a phase that changed that would have moved every existing caller.

The extracted sequence model agrees with the shipped `Ops.applyAllWith` and `Ops.canApplyAllWith` over generated scripts and a DRAWN `canHold`, drawn for the reason the per-operation container family draws one — the theorems quantify over the predicate, and a run against one hand-picked instance certifies that instance and nothing about the quantifier. Four things are compared and the last two are the sequence surface's entire contribution over the per-operation one: the verdict and the accepted tree through production's own `Tree.encodeHash`, the rejection class, the refusal INDEX, and the PARTIAL TREE the refusal hands back. Adequacy counts MID-script refusals separately and asserts them, because a refusal at index 0 returns the caller's own input and so compares the partial tree against nothing — measured at 24 trials, seed 1600: 45 scripts accepted, 123 refused, 60 of those mid-script, 103 of them NotAContainer, all 8 predicates drawn. The go-red is the model's own capability-free sequence check, which `container-sequence-gap` already proves to be a weakening, substituted into the dry-run slot and required to lose. Agreement is over the pool drawn, never over all inputs.
